findings.summary: Abstract algebra studies algebraic structures—sets equipped with operations such as groups, rings, fields, and modules—distinguished from elementary algebra by its focus on axiomatic systems rather than numerical computation. Emerging in the 19th century from number theory, geometry, and equation solving, it unified disparate results under common axioms like associativity and closure. Early development traced Galois theory, permutation groups, and ring classification, culminating in formal axiomatic definitions in the early 20th century that established the field's modern scope.

mechanisms.title: Axiomatic unification of algebraic structures
mechanisms.explanation: The field arose by collecting disparate mathematical facts into a common axiomatic core, defining structures such as groups, rings, and fields by formal properties like closure, associativity, and identity, then reformulating results within this abstract setting.

mechanisms.title: Historical emergence from concrete problems
mechanisms.explanation: Abstract algebra developed from specific domains—Galois theory from polynomial equations, group theory from symmetry and geometry, ring theory from number systems and matrix algebra—before being synthesized into a unified axiomatic discipline.
